final_message:
All three versions are written and pass every sample. Each one also matches an independent reference on 40 random inputs, 7 edge cases, and a benchmark-size input. The NumPy version is not as fast as I'd hoped, though.

**Files**
- `rust/src/main.rs` (plus a `[profile.release]` section in `rust/Cargo.toml`: fat LTO, one codegen unit, `panic = "abort"`). Builds offline with no warnings. None of the listed crates are used.
- `plain.py` (standard library only)
- `fast.py` (NumPy)

**Algorithm (same in all three)**
A word is a run of letters, lower-cased. A sentence end (`.`, `!`, `?`) clears the previous word. Each word after the first in a sentence forms a pair with its predecessor. Pair counts are then sorted by count, then by first and second word. The output is the 20 most frequent pairs.

**Speed choices**
- **Rust:** reads 1 MiB chunks, so the input is never held in memory. Words of up to 8 letters are packed into a `u64` and hashed with a small multiplicative hasher. Each pair is stored as one `u64` of word ids. Words are then ranked in byte order, so a pair key sorts exactly as the output needs. The keys go through an LSD radix sort, and the top 20 are picked in one pass over the sorted runs.
- **plain.py:** lower-cases once, splits on sentence punctuation, and extracts words per sentence with `re`. Pairs are counted with `Counter.update(zip(...))`, which runs in C. Only candidates at or above the 20th-highest count are sorted.
- **fast.py:** finds word boundaries with array differences and sentence breaks with `searchsorted`. Words are grouped by packing their bytes into `uint64` columns and running `np.unique` on a hash. Every word is then checked against its group's bytes, and a dict-based path handles words over 64 letters or any failed check. Pair keys are `uint32` ranks, sorted in NumPy, and the top 20 come from `partition` and `lexsort`.

**Results**
- Samples s1, s2, s3: all three versions match the expected output byte-for-byte.
- Random and edge cases (words up to 30 letters, digits, uppercase, empty input, no letters): all three match the reference.
- Benchmark-size input (66 MB, 9.8M words, 40k vocabulary): all three match the reference.

Timings are from a machine other programs were loading, so only the relative order is meaningful:

| Version | Time (quiet run) | Time (loaded run) | Peak working set (loaded run) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rust | ~1.2–1.4 s | 3.3 s | 165 MB |
| plain.py | ~11–12 s | 18.8 s | 1.4 GB |
| fast.py | ~9 s | 13.8 s | 1.0 GB |

**Caveats**
- `fast.py` is only modestly faster than plain, and it uses a lot of memory. I didn't finish optimizing it. My guess is that `np.unique` (a sort of about 10M hashes) and the per-byte packing loop dominate, but I didn't confirm that with a profile on the final code.
- Rust is not built with `target-cpu=native`, because the benchmark machine's CPU isn't known.
- The Python files write to the binary stdout. In text mode, Windows turned `\n` into `\r\n`, which broke the byte comparison.
- One of my hung test commands left a `python -` process behind. I stopped only my own PIDs (37343 and 37344) and left another session's processes alone.
- My scratch test files are deleted, but the empty `wordpairs/scratch` folder couldn't be removed because something holds it open. It can be deleted once that handle is released.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
